criteria.name: Introduction: mission concept and rationale - Include the following required information: • What is the spacecraft's primary mission? • Why is the mission needed? • How many spacecraft are used and why? • Who are the users (operator and customers)?
criteria.reasoning: Explains the reef-monitoring mission and its Australian benefit, gives a rationale for using one spacecraft, and identifies likely users and funding. The operator is not explicitly named, and the rationale and user discussion are not supported with literature consistently, so this falls short of the highest standard.

criteria.reasoning: The report has a recognizable structure, executive summary, contents, headings, figures, and tables. technical_issues.issue: The report names likely customer agencies but does not explicitly identify a mission operator; the Australian ground facility is not itself an operator.

The proposed Vega E launch and rideshare arrangement are speculative rather than a confirmed mission opportunity. Compatibility of the spacecraft and deployment into the specified orbit is not demonstrated.

The reported RAAN does not by itself indicate the launch facility's location; RAAN is an inertial orbital orientation. An epoch and a more complete state specification are needed to interpret the orbital elements.
The ascending-node local solar time is not specified. Sun-synchronism alone does not establish that the satellite will image the reef in daylight or on the descending leg.
The claim that the near-polar orbit passes over almost the entire Earth is overstated: at 97.79° inclination, the ground track reaches only about 82.21° latitude.

The sensor's swath, ground sample distance, spectral capability, and ability to detect bleaching through water are not established. The proposed 600 km altitude and fluid-lensing application therefore lack a demonstrated imaging-feasibility basis.
The access table includes a duplicated access period and inconsistent access numbering, which weakens confidence in the reported mean and total contact statistics.

The assertion that access frequency is maximized by selecting a facility close to the poles is not generally valid for this mission; access depends on orbit geometry, site latitude, elevation mask, and operational constraints.

The report first describes an EOL manoeuvre, then states the spacecraft has no thrusters and proposes a drag sail. Drag-sail sizing, deorbit time, and compliance with disposal guidance are not evaluated.

The report cites Wikipedia as a source despite the task's explicit exclusion, and its references are largely bare URLs without complete bibliographic information. Table citations such as [50]–[74] do not correspond to the listed bibliography.

overall: The report presents a coherent Australian reef-monitoring concept and uses STK outputs to support parts of the orbit and communications design. Several required topics are covered, but important design validation is missing, the EOL plan is incomplete, and the report has significant citation and figure/table presentation shortcomings.

feedback.summary: You present a coherent Australian reef-monitoring concept and use STK outputs to support parts of the orbit and communications design. Your report covers the main mission topics, but incomplete design validation, an underdeveloped end-of-life plan, and citation and presentation issues limit how persuasive and reliable the overall design is.

criteria.C1: Your Introduction explains the reef-monitoring purpose, Australian benefit, rationale for one spacecraft, and likely users, including CSIRO and BOM. To strengthen this already accomplished work, explicitly name the mission operator—the ground facility is not itself an operator—and support the mission rationale and user roles more consistently with literature.
criteria.C2: Your Launch, Orbit, Ground Control & Communications, and Mission Duration & EOL sections address the required topics and use STK outputs. To reach the accomplished level, validate launch and rideshare compatibility, specify a complete orbit including epoch and ascending-node local solar time, demonstrate sensor feasibility, and reconcile and evaluate the EOL plan. Image 1 and the access table do not provide sufficient reliable evidence for all claims.
criteria.C3: Your Conclusion links the sun-synchronous orbit and Mt Pleasant facility to the mission. To reach the accomplished level, draw specific conclusions from your design evidence, especially the access analysis, and explain how unresolved orbit, imaging, and disposal uncertainties affect mission feasibility.
criteria.C4: Your report has an Executive Summary, contents, headings, figures, and tables, giving it a recognizable structure. To reach the accomplished level, improve grammar and consistency, give figures and tables clear numbering and titles, and ensure in-text citations match complete references. The bibliography includes Wikipedia and citation numbers such as [50]–[74] that do not match the listed entries.

next_steps: Name the mission operator in the Introduction and distinguish the operator, ground-control facility, customers, and other users; add appropriate sources to support the mission need and user roles.

Strengthen the Mission Design with evidence: confirm launch and deployment compatibility, fully specify and interpret the orbit, establish sensor capability for the reef-monitoring task, and resolve the conflicting EOL manoeuvre and drag-sail descriptions with disposal-time analysis.

Audit the Ground Control & Communications results and the report presentation: correct duplicated or inconsistently numbered access periods, qualify claims about access frequency, and make figure/table labels and citations consistent with a complete, appropriate bibliography.
